variants.headline: {{cityName}} completes the {{building}}
body: Work on the {{building}} in {{cityName}} ended this week, and the crew has already cleared the site. The keeper walked the empty rooms at dusk, counting doors and trying keys. The work is in use from today.

variants.headline: Notice from {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is ready
body: Notice is given to all with business at the {{building}} in {{cityName}}: the work is finished and the doors open at first light. Visitors should come before dark until the lamps are hung. The keeper will keep a list for the upper floor.

variants.headline: Now fix the gutter
body: The scaffolding around the {{building}} in {{cityName}} came down on a wet morning, and half the street came out to watch. A girl in the crowd asked the foreman whether the roof would keep her dry. He said it had kept him dry all week, and she took that as a promise.

variants.headline: Another job for the builders of {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has its {{building}}, and the men who raised it are already asking what comes next. The foreman has kept his best hands on the payroll, a cost the city pays every quiet week. If the {{terms.civic.government}} has another site in mind, this is the season to break ground.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} puts money behind the {{building}}
body: Carts of dressed stone began arriving at the {{building}} in {{cityName}} before the frost was off the road. The city has paid into the work, and the crew now keeps two shifts on the scaffold. Shopkeepers along the lane say the noise starts earlier and ends later than it did last month.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} funds the {{building}}
body: Word from {{cityName}}: the {{building}} has received a fresh sum from the city chest, and wages will be paid through the winter. The stewards will post the account at the site each week. Tradesmen with stone or timber to sell should apply at the gate.

variants.headline: Why {{cityName}} is paying for the {{building}}
body: Money has gone into the {{building}} at {{cityName}}, and the first thing it bought was speed. The scaffold holds twice the hands it did a month ago, and the keeper now speaks of an opening day. The city chest is lighter for it, and the next project will wait its turn.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Coin speeds the {{building}}
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! The {{building}} has coin behind it now, and the masons work by lamplight! Stone by stone, the roof comes nearer! Come and see what your money is building!

variants.headline: {{cityName}} buys the {{building}}
body: There was no building season at {{cityName}}: the {{building}} was bought finished, and the city paid in {{currency}}. The first visitors found the mortar still damp and the keeper still looking for the keys. A line had formed at the door before the ink dried on the deed.

variants.headline: No wait in {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is bought
body: Other cities wait seasons for a {{building}} and watch every course go up. {{cityName}} did it in an afternoon: counted out {{currency}}, took the keys, opened the door. The masons who expected the work are still standing in the yard.

variants.headline: A purchase for {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is ready
body: It is confirmed that {{cityName}} has secured its {{building}} for {{currency}} and holds it ready for use. The bargain was settled in a single season, sparing the city a long spell of dust and scaffolding. The keys were handed over before the plaster was dry.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} pays for speed
body: {{cityName}} bought its {{building}} outright for {{currency}}, and the work was finished before anyone could watch it rise. Speed was the purchase, and the price is entered in the city books. What the same sum might have done elsewhere is not written down, which is how most bargains escape judgment.

variants.headline: {{largest}} outgrows the capital
body: The count in {{largest}} passed the capital this week, and the clerk who keeps the roll has ordered a longer table. The city now holds {{largestPopulation}} people against {{capital}}. For the first time, the realm's biggest crowd gathers outside the capital.

variants.headline: {{largest}} pass the capital
body: The roll has a tie at the top: {{largest}} each hold {{largestPopulation}} people, which puts every one of them past {{capital}}. A clerk in the capital has copied the figures twice to be sure. The table of city ranks has no first line, only a row of equals.

variants.headline: {{largest}} now outweighs {{capital}}
body: {{largest}} now holds more people than {{capital}}, and the {{terms.civic.government}} has not moved a chair. Petitions still go to the capital, and the clerks there still decide which to answer. In {{largest}}, the man who binds those petitions has asked for a bigger sack, a request that says more about the future than any census.

variants.headline: {{capital}} loses its crown to {{largest}}
body: In the market at {{capital}}, an old speaker still opens with the biggest city in the realm. A boy in the crowd has taken to shouting the new figure, {{largestPopulation}}, and naming {{largest}} at the top of his voice. The speaker has not changed his line, but he no longer waits for applause.

variants.headline: The capital just got outgrown
body: {{largest}} just passed {{capital}} on the population roll, {{largestPopulation}} people to the capital's smaller count. The {{terms.civic.government}} still sits in the capital. The crowds have other ideas.

variants.headline: The same grievance in {{count|city|cities}}
body: The same entry now heads the complaint books in {{count}} of our cities: {{key}}. Clerks in each town wrote it without knowing the others had. A grievance with that many addresses is a question for the capital.

variants.headline: One problem, {{count|city|cities}}
body: The entry {{key}} leads the complaint book in {{count}} of our cities, and a pattern that wide is policy by another name. Weather explains one bad season in one town; it does not explain the same line in every ledger. The {{terms.civic.government}} should be able to say when the choice was made and who expected to gain by it.

variants.headline: Hunger in {{count}} of our cities
body: Hunger now leads the complaint book in {{count}} cities. Ask anyone in a bread line and they will say it led there last month. The capital has the count now, and the capital can read.

variants.headline: Boredom in {{count|city|cities}}
body: The complaint is the same in {{count}} of our cities: nothing to do once the day's work is done. Benches in the square fill before dark and empty by the first bell. A fiddler in one of those towns has played the same three songs all summer, and nobody has asked for a fourth.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is being razed
body: Fire has been set to {{cityName}} by {{civilization}}, and the burning is deliberate. At the present pace, {{turns}} will pass before the walls are down and the site is bare. The roads that led there will be the only thing left.

variants.headline: {{population}} people remain as {{cityName}} is razed
body: {{population}} people are still inside {{cityName}} while {{civilization}} burns it street by street. No order has come to spare the place, and the fire has {{turns}} more to run. Families at the gate have stacked their bundles by the road and wait for a gap in the flames.

variants.headline: A city burns {{distance}} from our nearest city
body: Word from the frontier says {{civilization}} is burning {{cityName}}, {{distance}} from the nearest of our towns. Travelers from that country speak of smoke lying flat across the fields at noon. This office will print the next dispatch as soon as a rider reaches us.

variants.headline: The end of {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has {{turns}} before the last of it is gone, and the fire is the work of {{civilization}}. The city had its shrines and its market days, and both will end together. The prayers once said there will be said elsewhere, by people who remember the stones.

variants.headline: Flags change over {{cityName}}
body: This office has reported {{cityName}} changing hands more than once, and each report went to print as it arrived. {{merge.values.transfers}}{{merge.values.holder}} Folk there have learned to leave the gate unpainted until they are sure who holds it next.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is ours
body: Our soldiers took {{cityName}} from {{formerOwner}}, and our flag went up over the gate before the smoke cleared. The granaries, the walls and the people inside all passed to us with the city. The garrison that held it is gone, and the market has reopened.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{captor}}
body: {{captor}} has taken {{cityName}} from us. The garrison is broken, the gates stand open to their soldiers, and the oaths sworn there last season count for nothing. Runners carried the news out ahead of the closing roads.

variants.headline: What {{cityName}} adds
body: {{cityName}} brings walls, wells and a stretch of high ground, and it brings a people who did not choose us. Holding it means manning the gate, feeding the streets and watching the old loyalties for a season or two. An army can take a city in a morning; keeping it is the campaign that follows.

variants.headline: Who is taking names for {{cityName}}?
body: {{cityName}} is gone, and no one in authority has said who is to blame. On our street, a laundress asked three carters the price of carrying a letter across the new border; all three named a sum and none would promise delivery. Open a desk where families may leave letters, and use the road you found so quickly when there were taxes to collect.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} finishes new defenses
body: The last stone of the {{building}} went into place at {{cityName}} this week, and the gatekeeper has been trying the new bars ever since. Rubble still lies in the ditch, but the wall behind it would turn a raid today. The watch has moved its posts to the higher ground.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} strengthens its walls
body: Sentries at {{cityName}} climbed to their new posts this morning, now that the {{building}} is finished. The officer of the watch says any column coming up the road would need ladders it did not bring. The town sleeps easier, and the watch does not.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is ready for a siege
body: {{terms.civic.people}} of {{cityName}}, look up! The {{building}} is finished, stone on stone, and the watch has moved into it! Let the enemy count our walls from the road! Sleep easy tonight!

variants.headline: A stronger {{cityName}}
body: It is confirmed that the {{building}} at {{cityName}} is complete and the watch installed. The {{terms.civic.government}} ordered the work done before the danger was plain, and the city has the benefit of it now. Visitors will find the gate open at the usual hours.

variants.headline: Famine grips {{city}}
body: The bakeries of {{city}} are closing before noon, and the queues outside them form earlier each week. Famine now leads every other complaint in the city, leaving {{faminePopulation}} {{terms.civic.people}} unhappy. By the time the bread is gone, the square is empty.

variants.headline: Why {{city}} is hungry
body: {{city}} cannot feed itself, and the city's own count puts famine ahead of every other grievance. {{faminePopulation}} {{terms.civic.people}} are unhappy because of it. Granaries do not empty on their own; someone set the harvest, the stores and the roads, and someone should explain the result.

variants.headline: Empty stalls in {{city}}
body: A woman in {{city}} keeps a chipped bowl by her door for the bread cart. Last winter the cart came twice a day; now it comes once and is empty before she reaches the corner. She has stopped hurrying, she says, because hurrying does not bake bread.

variants.headline: A call for bread in {{city}}
body: The faithful of {{city}} are asked to bring what they can spare to the shrine steps before dark. Famine is the city's heaviest burden, and the stores must stretch to the next harvest. A loaf left at the shrine tonight will be on a table before morning.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} changes allegiance
body: The flag over {{cityName}} came down in the night and another went up by morning. The city has turned from {{formerOwner}} to {{newOwner}} without a treaty or a siege. Clerks at the town hall are already cutting new seals and scraping the old ones off the forms.

variants.headline: Old orders under a new flag in {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} changed hands without a battle, and the bill for that is usually paid at the customs house. Merchants hauling goods between {{formerOwner}} and {{newOwner}} now must learn a new set of duties, seals and officials. The first cart held at the gate will say more about the new order than any speech from the square.

variants.headline: Madam, we are {{newOwner}} now
body: Madam, the flag above our square is {{newOwner}}'s now, and the clerks have already changed the headings on every form. The people of {{cityName}} did not move: the same bakers, the same boatmen, the same children in the lane. We ask {{newOwner}} to encourage our trade and to be gentle with our taxes. The quarrel with {{formerOwner}} was never ours.

variants.headline: The flag changed overnight in {{cityName}}
body: The watchman on the east gate of {{cityName}} hauled down one flag and ran up another before breakfast, then went home to sleep. By noon the square held two crowds, one cheering {{newOwner}} and one muttering about {{formerOwner}}. The same baker sold bread to both and said nothing.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} reaches {{population}} people
body: A new lane has opened on the edge of {{cityName}}, and the washing lines are already up. The city now counts {{population}} people, which makes it a {{milestone}}. The council has begun to argue about where the next well should be dug.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} crosses {{population}}
body: {{cityName}} is now a {{milestone}} at {{population}} people, and the size changes what the city can ask of the realm. Its market runs past the afternoon bell, and the potters have fired a second kiln. More hands mean more trade, more noise and louder demands for roads and wells, and a city that answers those demands will not stay this size for long.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} has grown to {{population}}!
body: {{terms.civic.people}} of {{cityName}}, all hear it! The city counts {{population}} souls and stands now as a {{milestone}}! Count the chimneys and count the carts! Say the name aloud: {{cityName}}!

variants.headline: A milestone for {{cityName}}
body: We are informed that {{cityName}} has reached {{population}} people and is now reckoned a {{milestone}}. The older families will tell you the walk to the well has grown longer and the crowd at the market larger still. Such growth comes slowly, and the city is the sounder for it.

variants.headline: {{liberator}} liberates {{liberated}}
body: {{liberator}} drove the occupiers out of {{liberated}}, and the nation raised its own flag again before the day was over. A crowd gathered at the council hall and sang the old anthem twice, badly. The guard outside the door wears the nation's colors this morning.

variants.headline: Our independence is restored
body: Our long occupation is over. {{liberator}} restored the nation to its own government, and the council chamber that answered to a foreign governor answers to us again. The guard at the door has changed colors, and the first session is already called.

variants.headline: {{liberated}} is free again
body: {{liberated}} governs itself again. The nation that lived under a foreign banner raised its own this week, and its council has taken up the ordinary work of law and taxes. Messengers carried word through the streets that had waited for the old flag to return.

variants.headline: A nation restored: {{liberated}} is free
body: We are informed from {{liberated}} that the nation has taken up its own government once more, {{liberator}} having cleared away the foreign garrison. At the council hall a new seal was cut and the old one broken in the same hour. The returned government has sent its thanks, and our merchants may look for the roads to open.

variants.headline: Freedom for {{liberated}}
body: {{liberated}} flies its own flag again, and {{liberator}} made that possible. A nation restored is a friend for a generation; a nation swallowed whole is a grievance that outlives the men who ordered it. Remember which of the two {{liberator}} chose, and remember it the next time a map is redrawn.

variants.headline: Pillaged land weighs on {{city}}
body: Raiders stripped the land around {{city}} and left the farmsteads empty. Pillage is now the city's leading grievance, and it leaves {{pillagedPopulation}} {{terms.civic.people}} unhappy. The road that once carried vegetables to market carries dust.

variants.headline: The fields around {{city}} lie in ruin
body: The count of {{city}} puts pillage first among its troubles, with {{pillagedPopulation}} {{terms.civic.people}} unhappy. A raid takes a night; rebuilding takes seed, hands and a season. The officers who decide where the garrison stands should be asked why these fields were left open.

variants.headline: The road to {{city}} is empty now
body: The cart track south of {{city}} used to be busy before daybreak. Now the ruts are dry and the farms along it stand open to the wind, their doors gone for firewood. The families who worked them sleep inside the walls and walk out each morning to look at what is left.

variants.headline: {{city}} counts the cost of pillage
body: Word from {{city}}: pillaged land is now the heaviest burden on the city, and {{pillagedPopulation}} {{terms.civic.people}} are unhappy because of it. Towns with wagons, seed or labor to spare should send word to the council.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} holds with damaged defenses
body: {{cityName}} still stands, though its walls are badly broken. Families near the rampart have carried their bedding to relatives deeper in the city, and the market has moved into the narrow streets behind the wall. The gate is barred, and the watch does not sleep.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} holds against the siege
body: Hear me, {{terms.civic.people}} of {{cityName}}! The enemy is at the gate and the wall is battered, but it still stands! Bring water to the rampart and keep your fires low! Stand fast. The wall holds!

variants.headline: Can {{cityName}} repair its walls under siege?
body: {{cityName}} can hold for a while, but its wall cannot be repaired while the road is closed. Stone, lime and timber all come from outside, and an army at the gate takes the road first. The garrison's quiet days are its only chance to haul and mix, and it should spend them that way.

variants.headline: Life inside besieged {{cityName}}
body: In {{cityName}} the bakers have moved their ovens to the back rooms and the money is kept in aprons. Prices are chalked fresh at dawn and paid without argument. At night the city listens to one sound, the gate creaking on its hinges as the watch walks above it.

variants.headline: The defense of {{cityName}} continues
body: We are advised that {{cityName}} remains under siege, its walls sorely battered but still holding. The watch relieves itself without a gap, and runners are moving at all hours. Citizens are asked to keep the streets clear for them.

variants.headline: A new colony {{distance}} from the capital
body: The flag went up at {{cityName}} this week, {{distance}} from the capital and a long road from any help. The settlers spent their first night around a single fire, dividing the ground by rope and argument. The town will remember that first fire longer than it remembers us.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is a long way from home
body: {{cityName}} is {{distance}} from the capital, and that distance is now the town's chief fact. Grain, orders and soldiers will all come the same long way, and all will arrive late. A road will follow the settlers in time, and the road will bring the next town with it.

variants.headline: A new town, {{distance}} out
body: They have founded a town called {{cityName}}, {{distance}} out from home, and nobody asked the rest of us whether we wished to pay for it. The settlers are brave, or desperate, or both. This paper wishes them well and will be watching the accounts.

variants.headline: A colony at {{cityName}}
body: Advice reaches this office of {{cityName}}, founded {{distance}} from the capital and now open to trade. The settlement has a cleared site, a few shelters and little else as yet. Traders bound that way should ask the market office for the route and the return load.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} completes the {{building}} in {{cityName}}
body: The scaffold at {{cityName}} came down this week, and the {{building}} stands finished under {{civilization}}'s flag. Carts have been going in and out of the gate since dawn. Our watchers across the border counted them until dark.

variants.headline: New works at {{cityName}}
body: The {{building}} at {{cityName}} is finished, and {{civilization}} can now do something on this frontier that it could not do last season. That is the whole meaning of the news, and it is enough. Our own plans should be made on the assumption that the next work has already begun.

variants.headline: From beyond our border: {{cityName}} completes the {{building}}
body: We are informed from beyond the border that {{cityName}} has completed its {{building}} for {{civilization}}. The road to the city was busy all season and has been quiet since the roof went on. Traders bound that way will find the work finished and the crowds gone home.

variants.headline: A neighbor's new work
body: A carter who came through {{cityName}} last week swears the {{building}} was not there in spring. He has told the story in three markets, and each time the building gets taller. The people of the city only shrug and say it was finished before the rains.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} buys the {{building}} in {{cityName}}
body: No scaffold ever stood at {{cityName}}. The {{building}} was bought finished, and {{civilization}} paid for it in {{currency}}. The first visitors found the mortar still damp and the keeper still hunting for the keys.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} pays for the {{building}} near our border
body: At {{cityName}} the {{building}} was bought, not built: {{civilization}} paid and took it finished. A neighbor that buys its works outright has money to spare and a reason to want them sooner. Both deserve a line in our own accounts.

variants.headline: A neighbor's deep purse
body: A trader from {{cityName}} says he walked past a fenced pit in the morning and a finished {{building}} by evening. {{civilization}} paid in {{currency}} and skipped the years of dust, he says, and the market laughs. Nobody in the city finds it as funny.

variants.headline: Notice from {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is bought
body: Notice is given that the {{building}} at {{cityName}} has been bought complete by {{civilization}}, the price paid in {{currency}}. No building season was spent on it, and no scaffolding was raised. The city has the use of the work at once, and the sellers have the money.

variants.headline: A new town on the doorstep of {{ours}}
body: A new town called {{city}} now stands {{distance}} from {{ours}}, and {{player}} put it there. From the far field, our farmers can see its roofs and its smoke. The ground between the two towns is the first thing they will argue about.

variants.headline: {{player}} plants a town near {{ours}}
body: {{player}} has placed {{city}} {{distance}} from {{ours}}, and the site was chosen with care. A settlement that close can watch our road, shelter their patrols and crowd our fields without a single soldier in sight. The answer to a post is another post, and ours has not been built.

variants.headline: {{city}} rises beside {{ours}}
body: There is a new town called {{city}} {{distance}} from {{ours}}, and no one has told the farmers where their fields end. {{player}} drew the line on a map in some far room. Send surveyors before the harvest, or the first argument over a furrow will be settled with a scythe.

variants.headline: New neighbors at {{city}}
body: We are informed that {{player}} has founded {{city}}, a town {{distance}} from {{ours}} and close enough for a morning's ride. Such neighbors try the patience, but they also bring a market where our merchants may sell. It is cheaper to trade across a border than to guard it.

variants.headline: {{city}} comes under direct rule
body: {{city}} has stopped being a puppet and become a province, ruled directly from {{owner}}. The flag above the gate is the same, but every order now comes from the capital. The first sign will be the tax collectors, who no longer need to ask.

variants.headline: {{owner}} tightens its hold on {{city}}
body: A puppet bargains; a province obeys. {{city}} has just changed from one to the other, and {{owner}} now runs it from the capital. Lying {{distance}} from our nearest city, the change means decisions that once took a season may now take a week.

variants.headline: A puppet no more: {{city}} answers to {{owner}}
body: {{owner}} has folded {{city}} into its direct rule, and the city's men and grain now answer to the capital without the old bargaining. There was no ceremony worth reporting and no garrison change. The difference is in how fast an order travels.

variants.headline: A change of rule in {{city}}
body: Word is given that {{city}}, lately a puppet, now answers to {{owner}} directly. The garrison has not changed and the ceremonies were brief. What has changed is who may give orders, and how quickly they arrive.

variants.headline: Resistance continues in {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} is ours on the map, and nowhere else. Its clerks send out orders and then file them away when nothing happens, and the prefect expects {{turns}} more of the same. He has stopped promising an early end.

variants.headline: {{population}} people in an occupied {{cityName}}
body: There are {{population}} people inside {{cityName}}, and the city has not accepted the flag above the gate. The city is expected to resist for {{turns}} more, which makes the occupation a campaign with no enemy to fight. The men who ordered it owe the treasury an account of how it ends.

variants.headline: The old loyalty runs deep in {{cityName}}
body: In the market at {{cityName}}, a fishwife still gives her prices in {{formerOwner}}'s coin. Nobody in the queue corrects her, and the prefect's men walk past without a word. She says the city will need {{turns}} more of our rule before she learns the new money, and she does not sound hurried.

variants.headline: Mood darkens in occupied {{cityName}}
body: The occupation of {{cityName}} is entering another season, and the city's books put local happiness at {{unrestPoints}}. Patrols in the old quarter have been doubled. The prefect says {{turns}} more must pass before the city settles, a phrase he has used before.

variants.headline: A new city: {{cityName}}
body: The stakes went in at dawn, and by dusk {{cityName}} had a fire, a roped-off square and a name on the gate. Our settlers raised it under our flag. What comes next is the old list: houses, fields and walls.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{cityName}} is founded
body: Word for every street and every stall: {{cityName}} is founded! Our settlers raised the flag at dawn, and there is a new city under it! {{terms.civic.people}}, say the name and say it again: {{cityName}}!

variants.headline: {{cityName}} begins its story
body: Every city begins as a promise that someone has to keep. {{cityName}} has the site, the settlers and the flag, and nothing else that a hard winter respects. Seed and tools sent this season will decide whether the town is a city in ten years.

variants.headline: A new settlement at {{cityName}}
body: It is with pleasure that we record the founding of {{cityName}} under the nation's flag. The {{terms.civic.government}} has pledged the town protection and a share of the next stores. Settlers bound for the site may register at the capital.

variants.headline: Who pays for the sign in {{cityName}}?
body: Madam, my son has gone out to {{cityName}} and wants a sign for its first shop. The town, he writes, already speaks of itself as the equal of any in the country. Before I paint, tell me who settles its accounts, so the bill goes to a desk that will pay it.

variants.headline: Settlers ready as {{town}} grows smaller
body: The carts are loaded at the edge of {{town}} and the count is down. A settler party is ready to go, and the neighbors are already dividing the work the leavers will not do. Nobody has said aloud which families will be missed most.

variants.headline: Settlers ready, spirits low in {{town}}
body: {{town}} is smaller this week, and its temper is worse. The settler party took families out through the gate, and those who stayed find the streets no easier for the empty rooms. The council has offered no explanation.

variants.headline: Good cheer in {{town}} as settlers prepare to go
body: The settler carts left {{town}} this week, and the town is in good cheer. Tables are less crowded, the lanes are quieter, and the council points to the mood as proof the plan worked. It may even be true.

variants.headline: One more thing to pack in {{town}}
body: The carts on the east lane of {{town}} stand loaded past the axles, and the count is down by {{lost}}. A woman at the last door is giving away the pots she cannot carry and keeping one lid. Her neighbor, who has taken the hens, asks only that she take the rooster with her.

variants.headline: {{city}} is eating into its stores
body: The chalk line on the granary door in {{city}} drops a little every morning. The city holds {{foodStored}} and gives up {{shortfall}} of that each day, with no army outside to blame. The keeper has stopped chalking the good weeks, because there are none.

variants.headline: Why {{city}} is starving in peacetime
body: There is no siege at {{city}}, no raiders in the fields and no enemy at the gate. Yet the city loses {{shortfall}} of food a day from a store of {{foodStored}}, and the granary books say so plainly. Peacetime hunger is somebody's decision, and somebody should be asked to explain it.

variants.headline: The granary at {{city}} is emptying
body: A baker on the high street in {{city}} now cuts every loaf in two before she opens the shop. The granary holds {{foodStored}}, and it loses {{shortfall}} a day. She has stopped taking orders for next week, and her customers have stopped asking.

variants.headline: The food account of {{city}}
body: Grain in store: {{foodStored}}.
Lost each day: {{shortfall}}.
Siege: none. Battle: none. The store still falls.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is being razed
body: Our soldiers began pulling down the walls of {{cityName}} this week, and the smoke has not lifted since. {{turns}} will see the last of it. The road to the site is already quieter than it was.

variants.headline: The decision to raze {{cityName}}
body: The destruction of {{cityName}} will take {{turns}}, and when it is done the realm will have one fewer gate to hold and one more open field to watch. A razed city costs less to keep and more to explain. The order was ours; so is the empty ground.

variants.headline: The end of {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has {{turns}} before the last wall comes down and the ground is cleared. Its market days and its prayers will end in the same hour. The gods it served will have to remember it, because the fields will not.

variants.headline: {{population}} people and {{turns}} left in {{cityName}}
body: There are still {{population}} people inside {{cityName}}, and our soldiers are burning it around them. {{turns}} will empty the place one way or another. The busiest street in the city is the road out.
